lookAlikes.name: Cat's ear
lookAlikes.howToTellApart: Cat's ear has hairy leaves and solid, sometimes branched flower stems, while dandelion leaves are usually hairless and flower stems are hollow, unbranched, and contain milky sap.

lookAlikes.name: Hawkweed
lookAlikes.howToTellApart: Hawkweed often has hairy leaves and leafy flower stems with multiple flower heads, whereas dandelion has a basal rosette and solitary flower heads on leafless hollow stems.

identificationFeatures: Basal rosette of deeply lobed leaves with backward-pointing teeth
Bright yellow composite flower heads solitary on stems
White spherical seed heads with wind-dispersed achenes

threat.competitiveness: Moderate; competes for water, nutrients, and light, especially in thin lawns and garden beds.
threat.seedsPerPlant: Up to 2000-5000 seeds per plant per year
threat.toxicityNote: Not toxic; edible for humans and livestock when harvested from clean areas.
threat.regulatoryNote: Not generally regulated; considered a common weed in many regions.

controlWindow.bestTiming: Before seed set; best when soil is moist for hand removal of the taproot, or in early rosette stage.
controlWindow.preventSeedSet: Remove or mow flower heads before they turn to white seed puffs to prevent wind dispersal.

mechanical: Hand-dig or fork out the entire taproot, especially after rain when soil is soft.
Repeated mowing close to the ground to weaken the plant and prevent seed production.
Smother with cardboard, black plastic, or thick mulch for several weeks.
Solarize soil with clear plastic during hot sunny weather to kill roots and seeds near the surface.
cultural: Maintain a dense, competitive lawn or ground cover with proper fertilization and overseeding.
Mow regularly at a height that favors desirable grasses and prevents dandelion flowering.
Apply mulch in garden beds to suppress seedling establishment.
Avoid excessive soil disturbance that exposes bare ground for seed germination.
biological: No highly effective biological control is commercially available for garden use.
Grazing by goats, sheep, or rabbits can reduce top growth but will not eliminate established taproots.
organicApproved: Acetic acid (20% or higher) as a spot spray on young rosettes, avoiding desirable plants.
Corn gluten meal as a pre-emergence suppressant for seedlings in established lawns.
Flame weeding or boiling water for small rosettes in cracks and paths.
Repeated cultivation and hand removal before seed set.

notSafeOnThisCrop.note: Selective broadleaf herbicide; can damage broadleaf garden crops and desirable ornamentals. Spot treat only when safe.
Effective on dandelion but persistent in soil and can injure many garden plants. Avoid near sensitive crops.
Non-selective; kills or damages any contacted desirable plant. Use only as directed spot treatment in paths or before planting.
Controls many broadleaf weeds but residues can persist in compost and mulch, injuring sensitive garden crops.

resistance.advice: Rotate across HRAC groups and integrate mechanical removal. Do not rely repeatedly on Group 4 herbicides in the same area; hand-digging taproots remains highly effective.

usesAndBenefits: Young leaves are edible raw in salads or cooked as greens; older leaves become bitter.
Flowers can be used for fritters, wine, or jelly.
Roasted roots are used as a caffeine-free coffee substitute.
Medicinal uses include diuretic and digestive support, but consult a healthcare professional; avoid harvest from sprayed or contaminated sites.
Forage for rabbits, tortoises, and some livestock.
Safety caveat: people with latex allergies may react to dandelion sap; avoid plants from herbicide-treated areas.
